blocks.x: I'm Black, and I'm wondering how well you knew Louis Armstrong when he was alive.

I knew Louis Armstrong real well. I got known him from around 19... 20... 27 when I went to Chicago. Lee Collins' band went on an excursion from New Orleans, and Lee and Lurie were buddies from kids. And naturally, Louis, Lee searched Lurie out and went to an excursion which they used to give all during the summer. Illinois Central Railroad, Illinois Railroad would give excursions to Chicago because so many people from New Orleans had relatives in Chicago. And there were always a trainload of people who would go for a week or a week into Chicago to visit their relatives. Because that was the main line up to... about the Mason-Dixie lines. A whole lot of freedom the South still didn't have. Like all the Jim Crow things, it was much better in Chicago. But you still was going in the ghetto or a slum era or the South side where blacks were. You went to Chicago, but you went to black Chicago. But it was a happy feeling to go up there and see your folks who were up North. And naturally, Lee searched out Lurie and Lurie responded and came on out to the Royal Garden where we played a dance, a New Orleans dance.
First chance I got to see Lurie, but I had...
I knew a whole lot about him because my Uncle Paul Barberin was one of the pioneers who went to Chicago around... ...1919, 1920.
Did he go to Chicago?

No, he went alone. He had a sister who lived up there and he went up there and there was a... There weren't many musicians around Chicago who were playing New Orleans type jazz. Only the ones who left here. What year was this? I'm talking about from... Up until say 23, there was nobody playing authentic New Orleans jazz in Chicago but New Orleans musicians. Because they had a whole lot of work around there like theater. Chicago was the most populous... I'd say it was about the second most populous section for black people in the country. It was a great migration point where people went off from Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas. You could walk to Chicago. Just keep walking if you had enough muscles in your legs. Just follow the track straight up. Many youngsters hoboed their way and just walk and hitch the ride and hitchhiked and went to Chicago. Especially in the summertime, you know. Not to hear the music. They went to better conditions. Working in the stock yard. Doing labor and work. Other than picking cotton and other things you did down south on the agricultural scene. You went to Chicago. You could work in Gary, Indiana. Steel Mills. And you did heavy manual labor. There was plenty of work. For whites and poor blacks who didn't have education. So there was a great influx of black New Orleans people and whites who went to Chicago. Everybody, New Orleans boasts of a relative who was in Chicago with a great many who went west to California. So Lee Collins met Lurie. Lurie came to the Royal Garden and there was a big table, a big party, and they sat down and he introduced everybody in the band to Lurie. Lurie was all glad to see Lurie. Lurie was a sensational celebrity of that time and the people just went wild and Lurie entered the door screaming and howling. We played and at that time Lurie had records out.
Excuse me Danny, what was the name of the band you were with then?

I was with Lee Collins, Jones and Collins. Astoria Band. We played at Astoria. We played in New Orleans on Rampart Street which was owned by Beansy Furrier. It had once been owned by, I can't think of a man's name. It was a brewery people. Beansy took it over. It was a gambling concession. and we worked there. And Professor Cook was the emcee in musical and performance director and everything. He was the wheel around there. So he staged this train excursion to Chicago, and we had our band to play. I had been to Chicago in 23 as a kid to visit my aunt. And me and my little uncle, we used to sneak around in the nightclubs and peep through the side windows, lay on our stomachs and look down in the cellars at the people bawling like, you know, 8 o'clock in the morning, you know, and look down at the cabarets. And naturally, being from a musical family, we knew about this club. One particular was called Idlewild, which was on State Street. And a guy named Ollie Powell, Ollie Powell, he worked there. He was a singing drummer. He was a big favorite. He and Tony Jackson around Chicago during that period. I was about, see, 21, 22, 23, I was around. I was about 12, 13 years old. I had a little uncle. He was 14, 15. He and I were real tight. That's Paul's younger brother. The drummer, he played trumpet, and I picked up the guitar, ukulele, the guitar, and banjo, and guitar later. And we would stroll. We'd get up early, like, you know, 6.30 in the morning, and we'd go walk the streets looking for pennies and nickels, seeing this walk to gutters. And pick up, man, you know, 50, 60 cents apiece. People drop money on the sidewalk. And he had eagle eyes, man. He could spot money. The father of me says, keep your eye on watch, and we see pennies and nickels. State Street was very populous with black people seeing, you know, money. Okay. So we used to go and peep in this particular cabaret. It was in the cellar, and the window was just about a foot above, say, two feet above, ground level. On the side entrance, we'd go there on our stomachs and look down in the nightclub at the people. Everybody boozed up down there, and you could cut the smoke in there. You know, you could see, and you'd see this drumming entertainers, how they were acting. They couldn't see us, but we could see them, see. And we'd lay down looking. And there was new us coming from New Orleans that time in the morning. Our parents didn't know, they'd see where we were going. My uncle would say, let's go and look at the cabaret. So we'd go down the state, I think, in 46th Street. And there was this club. And we'd go around the side and look down and lay on our stomach maybe about 40, 50 minutes. And we'd be watching the hustlers and the underworld characters with the chicks shaking and taking money off the tables between their legs, you know, the pop bottle deal. And, well, that's the Chicago I'd seen then. And then Louis Armstrong came to the Royal Garden that night when we arrived and I'm sitting on the bandstand. And there was another band that was playing there. It was two bands. The Union, you had the Baha'i Union Band. It was a Chicago band playing about eight pieces and our band. It was somewhat of a battle of music. But we was playing this new old funk and New Orleans music and them people were dancing to it and they would sit out when the other band would play. No, I don't need a match. I'm just a habit. Louis came in, man, and he sat at the table which was seated right in front of the, right in front of the bandstand and intermission. We all met him and everybody, all the hustlers, all the racketeers and all the pimps and all the cats that were doing good from New Orleans with their cheeks. There was, Chicago's a fast town. A lot of underworld activity and nightlife and people who live, you know, a fast life. And particularly the ones who had migrated from Storyville, Black Red Light District went to New Orleans and they were up there finger-popping, talking loud, drawing the crowd, you know, flashing money. and they all were around Louis' table and they begged Louis to play. And Louis said, well, yeah, okay, give me the horn. So I'm sitting there and there's this guy's trumpet there. He said, hammer that horn, my boy. Boom, down, hammer that horn. So I had him, I just picked up the horn and handed him the horn. So he picked up the horn and said, what you gonna play? He sat down at, he stood up at the table he was at, in front of us, down. We were up on a high bandstand about four or five feet high. And Louis was in the table below. And, uh, they, somebody howled out a player, uh, uh, When You Smilin', which was a big hit at that time. So he went into When You Smilin', he played it. And he didn't have a mic, but the band was real soft and he sang it. And the house went in their uproar, man, about, you know, like, seven, 800 people to a thousand people to scream for more. And he played something else. And then he handed me back the horn. So I put the horn back. So after that, man, there was pandemonium in the house begging to play more and all the catch cards. So, Lee Kahn said, let's get off the bandstand. So while I'm getting off, this trumpet player came on and he said, who gave Louis Armstrong my horn? He didn't say it loud. I said, I ain't no horn. He said, well, God damn, who gave you permission to let him blow my horn? I don't let nobody blow my horn. I don't care who it was. If it was Gabriel, nobody blows my horn, nobody puts their lips on my mouthpiece. I don't know where people's mouth been at. One of them kind of things, see? So, I said, well, excuse me, the lawyer asked me for the horn. And I didn't think it was, to me, it was like, you know, the greatest thing ever could happen to play the horn because that horn was never blowed before, since, you know, the horn must have been felt real good after Armstrong blew it if it had any, if we're having feelings of having been blowed by the boss, the king.
Yeah.

So, he scowled at me, he said, so your sons of bitches take, you son of, some son of bitches, he said, take too many liberties with people. He was mad because lawyer had played, see? I don't think it was so much about the horn. And, I used to know his name, I can't think of his name. He was one of those supposed to be hot trumpet players, right? She called him. And, and, that was the thing with lawyer everywhere, I mean, where he went. Guys who were celebrated in their hometown as being great trumpet players after lawyer came through there, playing like, you know, playing that big, beautiful tone, playing so beautiful. And, Lala, if you caught him, if you're in a mood and you play Tiger Rag or Chinatown, 50, 60 choruses, you know, wiping his chops with that handker and blowing, exhilarating excitement the way he could, well, most trumpet players, they couldn't take it. They professed that, they loved it, but deep down inside, you know, they couldn't come up with that thing, see?
Do you think, do you think that it bothered most of them that he was that good or do you think they really felt a legitimate warmth and passion for the way he played?

A lot of them had a passion and not, he was such a dominant figuring on trumpet playing, particularly amongst black musicians and white, and then white, but amongst blacks, ones who had, who, who, who, who, who could absorb the soul of what he played and had been around, exposed to the lifestyle he had, could relate to what he was playing and, and a whole slew of, of trumpet players, black trumpet players, received some acclaim by even just playing his solos. It ain't, maybe not to the same perfection, but just playing his solos off of records and if you could learn to play, say, a dozen or so of Lewis, great, exceptionally great solos and adopted, you had a style there, which was international style acclaimed by everybody. so you wasn't, you was in business if you just could play. I'm talking about in the early 30s and, from 30 to 40, oh man, I could call trumpet players until next week. Who, their solos and their whole style was based on, on Armstrong and there was other, a lot of whites as of today. They'll never mention Armstrong, they're all Bix fans because they relate to Bix by the Bix. and, you'll never mention Louis, but Bix because they were, there was two styles parallel to one another. They were about the same age and they both came up but unfortunately Bix died but he left for Legislative 2 and a, and a whole slew of great records. Now,
what was the difference in their style?

Well, there's a big difference. one was lyrical which from, from a classical vein, technically musical because Bix was a, uh, was interested in concert music and Debussy and Ravel and his thing was semi-classical, that In the Mist and a couple of piano pieces he wrote which had a, a great significance of creative inventiveness but based from a European, a classical vein where Louis stuff was so black out of the Baptist Church and out of the honky tonks and, uh, out of, uh, a tradition of New Orleans trumpet playing from Buddy Petit, Freddie Keppard, Bunk Johnson, Buddy Bowling, Freddie Keppard, Buddy Petit, and all these guys and he heard them, Manny Perez, he heard the best he knew, Papa C, he heard everybody here and at that time they were great trumpet players and he, I was all about there, he, he came out of that which is nitty-gritty black American earth lifestyle. Yeah. See, and some of his records attest to that like, in tunes like Drop That Sack, Potato Head Blues, Skip The Gutter,
Strutting With Some Barbecue.

Strutting With Some Barbecue, uh, and then the Fats Waller tune and Amos Behem, What Did I Do To Be So Black and Blue, and, uh, Dr. Jazz and Willie the Weeper, all them things were tunes that were Native American with a flair of the field and the, and the voice of what people in America did. See, Vicks had another thing going.
How would you, how would you compare the two of them with Joplin? Would Joplin sort of be in the middle and the way he,
Joplin?
Yeah, create ragtime.
Oh, Joplin's something else. Louie's not ragtime.
I realize that.
Louie's stomp down. Louie's, Joplin is a classical thing taken from Chopin, some things that Chopin has done, that type of two-handed piano. Technical, trained piano. That is Joplin. That's ragtime.
But, I mean, where do you see the black influence in Joplin? The way it influence is?

Well, it was a dance, you could tell, like ragtime and kickwalk dancing, like the Juba dance. Like the Juba dance. That was, uh, Joplin, you know, the hoedown, all those things of, of that particular time. Uh, they had, you know, dances. Because each generation have its dances to go with its music and its lifestyle. Well, Joplin, his music is spirited music, you know, of a, of a machine type. Or when you play ragtime, it's just like you put a piano roll on, you know? And, it's, it's, uh, a thing like Off to the Races. You got it?
Mm-hmm.
Well, like Jellarole, who came later, was somewhat funky. He taken ragtime and slowed it down. He called it stumps. Stomp down. It was too fast for,
Yeah,

see, he stole, he, uh, Shreveport stomp and, uh, Milenburg jars. Them things were slower, slower tempo. Why, what's the big hurry? In other words, you're telling ragtime. Slow it down. That's why Jellarole claimed he created jazz. Well, he did create what he created. Yeah. You understand? Yeah. And it's a misunderstood thing. Nick LaRocca say, he claimed he created jazz. Well, what he, the songs he created or what he lifted or whatever it was from other melodies, that was a sound that was around in New Orleans, what he created and put on a record, he claimed, in them days, you didn't have press agents. You understand? So you had to blow your own horn. If you'd done something that was yours, see? Just a, just a niche of something, you taking that and saying, this is mine, I created that. Jellarole didn't say anything. You see, I wrote this series of stomps, 15 to 20 or 30 tunes, and the people like it, King Porter's stomp and them kind of things. Well, that's mine. I created that. See? I created jazz. I think he got a thing, something, something about Dr. Jazz. And, I mean, like them, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, Paul Moretz, them, the things they recorded, which was during that period or a little later, they could have said, we created jazz. You understand?
Yeah.
There was a thing that they didn't have press. Nowadays, nobody say they create nothing. The press agent does it. But then them days, a musician, had to do it himself.

Seeing as how Armstrong, can you hold it over here soon? Did I just want to give it a hand? Seeing as how, you know, Armstrong went up to Chicago and made a big name for himself, in a way, he sort of put himself above that, all that competitiveness and savage competition when he became famous. And I'm just wondering if, do you think he ever took his fame for granted or was he always trying to expand it?

No, he was a happy man. He, he was so acclaimed by everybody. Every trumpet player, everybody who, who, who played a horn, paid him homage somewhere or other, or they stayed a distance from him. Whole lot of great white trumpet players, legitimate trumpet players, never went near Louis. You dig, they may have looked, but they dismissed him as, not exactly black, but that kind of style, that ain't, well, that's something to do with it too, but you always, you don't always put it on being black. He could have been white and they would ignore them. They got whites who would ignore Bix in preference of Lurie or Henry Bussey or Tony, Lurie Pinnico, you dig, B.A. Rolf. There are the trumpet players who were in the concert field, like B.A. Rolf, and you heard of B.A. Rolf. Oh, I had a big band one time. And they had these guys with the Ringling Brothers Circus, great technical concert cornet players, triple tongue artisan, and play high range, you know, and, and they dismissed, they never went near Armstrong, you know, because they couldn't conceive what the hell he was playing lots of times. It was funky black music. You dig? Unless you went in the story of a hunky-tonk and see Lurie how he could captivate black people doing this thing, all whites who got the message, like the white kids today have got the message of doing all the black dances that the rocks do. It's one of them things. But Lurie never looked back to, to, to claim nothing. At the same time, Lurie, before Lurie, there was Johnny Dunn, who had this extremely long trumpet, and he used to boast, I'm the greatest trumpet player that ever lived. I'm the king of the trumpet. He was called king, Johnny Dunn, played with Mamie Smith. And so far, he went to prove he was king, he went to Chicago to challenge Lurie. And reputed to have, went to the band, said, say, hand me that horn, boy. Show you how to play that horn. And Lurie handed him the horn, and he played, and when he got through, Lurie got angry, was angry about it, and said, take your horn and blow him out of here. And Lurie just proceeded to play Tiger Rag, maybe a hundred chorus, which, Johnny Dunn probably couldn't play, maybe a half a dozen.
Was Johnny Dunn from New Orleans?

No, he's from, he was from Memphis. But he was famous around New York. He was starring Broadway shows, like Little Lesson's Blackbirds, and some of them shows, and he played extra long trumpet about three feet long. And he sat in the pit, and he blew, like for the chorus girls when they come out. It was exciting to see him stand up and blow. And there's some records you could hear him, things he did, but nothing with the technique and the power and the drive and the beauty of Armstrong.
Did you know Papa Joe Oliver?
Yes, I knew Joe Oliver. Do you think, I mean, some people,

some people have indicated that he really wanted Louis to stay with him in Chicago when Louis left and went to New York, and that I think Lil Armstrong, his wife, his second wife, sort of had an influence on his leaving the band. Do you think there was any bitterness on Joe's part when Louis left to go to Chicago?

Oh, that's not no bitterness. I don't think there was no, there was no bitterness, but it was a sort of a, a loss to Joe because there was a tradition in New Orleans to have two trumpets in the band. Papa Celestine had two, at one time, Manny Perez had two, first and second trumpet. And, uh, other bands around had two trumpets, and you played second. And it was guys, it's just like baseball, a second string catcher, you dig, more than one pitcher, and, uh, or more than one quarterback in a, a football team. It was a thing. And, uh, like, Joe was up in age, like most trumpets who had gotten age, up in age, well, they didn't have the fire, or they didn't want to blow themselves to death, so they brought in a youngster and let him blow a second, like, Bunk Johnson lots of times sat in with Bolden, see? Uh, Ricard Alexis and, uh, Moeys Durant sat in with Manuel, Manuel Perez. Shots, Madison sat in with Papa Celestan. You got it? It was a tradition. When, when, when, when, when Lurie left, Joe Oliver imported Lee Collins. He tried to get Kid Rene. Younger trumpet players to come and play the second. I'm, you know, I'm the boss, but here's somebody, you know, it was a thing. It was a fraternal thing about him, you know, two peas in a pod, and I get another, like a relief. But in other words, you could make your name with a big band. To, it was to your advantage. To be playing in a, at a band, leader, which was a band, with a leader who was tenant to business, had an organized band in the top spot in New Orleans or playing for the top people. To play in a band, it was constantly an evolution of going up a step high, graduating.
Do you think,
there was some, a feeling, I guess, you know, he was glad to, he was sorry to leave Louie, because he and Louie was the famous duets they did, you dig?
Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive?

Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular, but to actually have, he moved around too fast. See, if he just stayed like, in Chicago, and worked in clubs, they stationary, like you make a reputation in the town, like Fletcher Henderson was in New York, Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club, Fletcher at the Roseland, you heard him on the radio, Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio, Earl Hines in, in the Grand Terrace in Chicago for a period of eight to ten years, you understand? Standard, Chick Webb, Savoy, Borrow for six, seven, eight years, you dig? When you stay in a spot in the town, then you get a following, but Jelly played in Chicago, I don't know how many big spots he played, then he moved out maybe to Wisconsin, and take a group and go to Kansas City and stay here, then he go to California, he was everywhere, so his records were popular, and his music, his songs, lasted, but far as him having a following of, of saying, well I got, you know, everybody, like when he come to New York, he was lost because, nobody knew Jelly in New York, you know, like a personal thing, to have a charisma, and people flock to you, seeing what his, his attitude, you know, he was sharp, you know, and he, he wasn't the guy that, uh, give you a whole lot of thank you, you know, thank you for signing all this, now you're going to hear something, you see, he's, he's, pretty arrogant guy, wasn't he? He wasn't that, he was sure of himself, not arrogant, but you said, that's arrogant, and he said, now I will present to you, this great thing I wrote, and his juicy marching on it, I'll present to you, listen that, listen closer to this, something you never heard before, fool, come here, and get, stand close, and, that's the way, with his lifestyle, confidence in himself, you understand, people misunderstood that, you suppose, it'll be quiet, sign autographs, nice and sweet, like, garland bottom, and thank you, and I will like, Duke, and I love you madly, you know, and, you know, and,

do you think that, do you think that, that Louis Armstrong, was able to, keep his reputation, even though he traveled, or do you think that he built, his reputation in Chicago, and then when he traveled, it was already behind him?

No, each record he, every, each record Louis ever made, was a, was a classic, and a lesson, to other musicians, his singing, his man didn't have, a tenor voice, or a baritone voice, you understand, he had a, Armstrong voice, but he had something, in his voice, which is, earthy, see, he could take tunes, like, you know, like the peanut vendor, who the hell, would have recorded, peanut vendor, and he taking a tune, like that, which in Broadway, when song were out, is, it's called a dog tune, see, the way, the way he done it, you understand, he take pennies from heaven, every time it rains, pennies from heaven, what he done to it, it's like lately, taking a tune, was a Broadway show, didn't expect the show, to go to Broadway, it's on the road, hello dolly, and the guy, brought him a tune, and he done, hello dolly, or, now if you hear, hello dolly, the way it actually is written, hello dolly, well hello dolly, it's so nice, a little timid, nice little thing, he took it,
hello dolly,
well hello dolly, give it a big dolly, and the way he's singing, he swung it,
yeah, yeah,

you understand, there's another, and the tune, became a smash hit, and the show, became a big success, well, just to hear, dolly, to see who the hell, was dolly in the show, on account of, Louis Armstrong, singing the song,
yeah, that's amazing,

well, I'm telling you, that's what he could do, with a tune, and each tune, Louis ever done, was a lesson, if it was a, a hit tune, out of a Broadway show, or popular tune, Stardust, and if you done it like Louis, it was accepted, by the public, and you learned something, his interpretation, of his horn playing, on the record, his ending, his beauty, of interpreting the tune, also singing it, with this voice of his, it was a raspy voice, like somebody with a coal, but it was so human, he's responsible, for the thing, that they call the D, song stylists, they had no song stylists, before Louis Armstrong, come on the scene, if you look on the records, in the 20's, you always see behind,
so that is
